segments.title: What makes a multi-train railway journey reliable
segments.body: At Newton Abbot, trouble on the journey home from London Paddington invites a comparison with a much longer rail journey between Sasebo and Hakodate. The Japanese trip took about fourteen hours and used six trains, with each connection working. Missing train managers and drivers, unavailable spare parts, and the effects of an earlier accident caused repeated Great Western Railway cancellations. By Newton Abbot, about halfway home in travel time, the disrupted trip may already have involved more trains than the entire Japanese journey. Station staff receive praise for being professional, kind, and helpful, so the criticism falls on the system rather than them. Railway reliability here depends on staffing, maintenance, incident recovery, and coordination between connecting services.

evidence.note: Clarke contrasts a smooth fourteen-hour, six-train journey in Japan with GWR cancellations attributed to staffing, spare parts, and an earlier accident, while praising station staff.

segments.summary: A disrupted GWR journey provides a direct comparison with a smooth 14-hour, six-train trip across Japan and separates frontline service from system reliability.
